units.title: Start Here
units.summary: How the Reading and Writing section works and the approach you'll use on every question.

lessons.title: How SAT Reading and Writing Works
objectives: Know the section's format, timing and four domains.
Use the same four-step approach on every question.
Recognize the four wrong-answer families.

blocks.content:
## The section at a glance
- **54 questions in 64 minutes**, in two 32-minute modules of 27 questions. That's about **71 seconds per question**.
- **Every question has its own short passage** (25–150 words), sometimes with a table, graph or a pair of texts.
- Each module has 2 unscored pretest questions you can't identify. Treat every question as real.
- Module 1 is a mix of difficulties. Your performance there decides whether Module 2 is harder or easier.

## The four domains
| Domain | What it tests | Units |
|---|---|---|
| Information and Ideas | main ideas, evidence, inferences | Unit 1 |
| Craft and Structure | words in context, purpose, paired texts | Unit 2 |
| Expression of Ideas | transitions, notes questions | Unit 3 |
| Standard English Conventions | grammar and punctuation | Unit 4 |

Questions of the same type are grouped together, so you'll see a run of vocabulary questions, then a run of evidence questions, and so on. Grammar and writing questions come later in each module.

## The approach for every question
1. **Read the question first** so you know what you're reading for.
2. **Read the passage** and **predict** the answer in your own words.
3. **Eliminate** using the wrong-answer families below.
4. **Choose** the answer that matches your prediction and has no flaw.

**The four wrong-answer families**
| Family | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Too extreme | only, always, never, proves, all |
| Off-topic | an idea the text never discusses |
| True but doesn't answer | an accurate detail that isn't what the question asks |
| Half right | starts correctly, then adds one wrong claim |

units.title: Information and Ideas
units.summary: Main ideas, textual and graphical evidence, and logical inferences.

lessons.title: Central Ideas and Details
objectives: Predict the main idea in your own words before reading the choices.
Find a specific detail the text states.
Eliminate with the four wrong-answer families.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
- The main idea is **what the whole text is mostly about**, including its point of view, not just its topic.
- Many passages turn: "Many assume… **however**…" The idea after the turn is usually the main idea.
- **Predict before you look.** A one-sentence summary in your own words protects you from attractive wrong answers.
- Detail questions ask what the text **says**. The answer is stated, often reworded.

## Worked example
> For decades, historians assumed that the weavers of Calderon Valley worked alone, each family guarding its own patterns. Recent analysis of 300 surviving textiles by researcher Imani Okafor, however, found the same rare dye recipes and border designs in villages miles apart. Okafor argues that the weavers likely shared techniques through a regional trading network.

**Which choice best states the main idea of the text?**
**Predict:** New evidence suggests the weavers shared techniques instead of working alone.

- A) Calderon Valley weavers invented the region's most famous dye recipes. *(Off-topic: who invented them isn't discussed.)*
- B) Okafor's analysis of textiles suggests weavers in Calderon Valley exchanged techniques, challenging an earlier assumption. ✅ *(Matches the prediction.)*
- C) Okafor studied 300 textiles from the region. *(True but doesn't answer: a detail, not the main idea.)*
- D) Okafor proves that every family in the valley belonged to a trading network. *(Too extreme: "proves," "every.")*

lessons.title: Command of Evidence: Textual
objectives: Identify exactly what a claim says, part by part.
Choose the finding or quotation that supports, weakens or illustrates it.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
These questions give you a **claim** (a hypothesis or an interpretation) and ask which evidence would **support**, **weaken**, or **illustrate** it.
1. **Find the claim** and restate it simply.
2. **Break it into parts.** "Bees prefer blue flowers **in cool weather**" has two parts: blue flowers, and cool weather.
3. **The right answer matches every part.** Wrong answers match only one part, or are about the right topic but the wrong relationship.
4. **Weaken** questions want evidence pointing the opposite way.
5. **Quotation questions** (poems and novels): find the line that shows the exact quality the claim names.

## Worked example
> Ecologist Tomas Ferreira hypothesizes that the small lizards on Pell Island change color mainly to control their body temperature rather than to signal to other lizards.

**Which finding would most directly support Ferreira's hypothesis?**
**The claim's parts:** color change happens for temperature, not for signaling.

- A) The lizards change color more often during the breeding season. *(Points toward signaling: weakens.)*
- B) The lizards turn darker on cool mornings and lighter in the afternoon heat, even when no other lizards are nearby. ✅ *(Temperature link AND rules out signaling.)*
- C) Lizards on Pell Island are smaller than those on the mainland. *(Off-topic.)*
- D) Some lizards on Pell Island can change color within seconds. *(True about color change, but says nothing about why.)*

lessons.title: Command of Evidence: Quantitative
objectives: Read tables and graphs quickly and accurately.
Pick the choice that is true to the data AND supports the claim.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
1. **Read the question and the claim first.** Usually the last sentence of the passage says what the data should show.
2. **Read the graphic's title, axes, labels and units.**
3. For each choice, check two things: **Is it true according to the data?** and **Does it support the claim?**
4. The trap is a choice that reads the graph correctly but doesn't connect to the claim.

## Worked example
> A city council member claims that the new bike lanes on Harbor Street made cycling there more popular.

| Year | Daily cyclists on Harbor St. | Daily cyclists on Pine St. (no new lanes) |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 (before lanes) | 140 | 150 |
| 2023 (after lanes) | 310 | 160 |

**Which choice best uses the data to support the claim?**
- A) Pine Street had more cyclists than Harbor Street in 2021. *(True, but doesn't support the claim.)*
- B) Daily cyclists on Harbor Street more than doubled after the lanes were added, while Pine Street stayed about the same. ✅ *(True and directly supports it.)*
- C) Both streets had fewer than 200 cyclists in 2023. *(False: Harbor had 310.)*
- D) Harbor Street had 310 daily cyclists in 2023. *(True, but alone it doesn't show a change.)*

lessons.title: Inferences
objectives: Follow a passage's logic to the conclusion it sets up.
Pick the choice that must be true, not one that merely could be.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
"Which choice most logically completes the text?" questions give you a chain of reasoning with the last link missing.
1. **Number the steps** of the argument: what's established, what's ruled out, what's left.
2. **Predict the conclusion** before reading the choices.
3. The answer is usually **modest**: the smallest statement the text forces. Choices that go beyond the evidence are wrong, even if they sound smart.

## Worked example
> Archaeologists at the Renwick site found charred seeds of a grain that grows only in warm, wet climates. Pollen records show that the region has been cool and dry for the past 4,000 years, but was warm and wet before then. Therefore, the charred seeds were most likely ______

- A) brought to the site by traders from a warmer region. *(Possible, but the text doesn't point there.)*
- B) left at the site more than 4,000 years ago. ✅ *(The grain grew there only when the climate was warm and wet.)*
- C) the main food source of everyone who lived in the region. *(Too extreme.)*
- D) burned during a recent wildfire. *(Contradicts the logic: the recent climate couldn't grow the grain.)*

units.title: Craft and Structure
units.summary: Words in context, text structure and purpose, and connections between paired texts.

lessons.title: Words in Context
objectives: Predict a word from context clues before reading the choices.
Choose the word that matches both meaning and tone.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
1. **Cover the choices.** Read the sentence with the blank.
2. **Find the clue:** a contrast word (but, although), a cause (because, so), a restatement after a colon, or an example.
3. **Predict your own word,** even a simple one ("good," "changed").
4. **Match meaning AND tone.** A positive context needs a positive word.
5. Watch for common words used in an unusual sense ("a **novel** approach" means new).

## Worked example
> The committee expected the proposal to be controversial, but it was approved with almost no debate; members found its reasoning so ______ that few saw any point in objecting.

**Clue:** "approved with almost no debate," "few saw any point in objecting." **Predict:** convincing.
- A) obscure *(would cause debate)*
- B) compelling ✅
- C) tentative *(weak, not convincing)*
- D) lengthy *(says nothing about how convincing)*

lessons.title: Text Structure and Purpose
objectives: Describe what a whole text does, or what one sentence does in it.
Match function verbs (introduces, challenges, illustrates) to the passage.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
These questions ask **why** something is there, not what it says.
- **Overall purpose:** describe the text's job in a sentence that starts with a verb: *to present a finding and explain why it surprised researchers.*
- **Function of a sentence:** look at what comes before and after. Does it give an example, raise a problem, offer a counterpoint, or state a conclusion?
- Every part of the right answer must be true. A choice that gets the first half right and the second half wrong is **half right**.

## Worked example
> Most bird species that live in cities sing at higher pitches than members of the same species in the countryside. **In one study, city robins sang nearly an octave higher than rural robins.** Researchers think the higher songs are easier to hear over the low rumble of traffic.

**What is the function of the underlined (bold) sentence?**
- A) It offers a specific example of the pattern described in the first sentence. ✅
- B) It challenges the claim made in the first sentence. *(It supports it.)*
- C) It explains why city birds sing at higher pitches. *(That's the third sentence.)*
- D) It introduces a new topic unrelated to the first sentence. *(Off-topic.)*

lessons.title: Cross-Text Connections
objectives: Summarize each text's position in one line.
Predict how one author would respond to the other.

blocks.content:
## Key ideas
1. **Read Text 1** and write its main claim in a few words.
2. **Read Text 2** and do the same.
3. **Name the relationship:** agree, disagree, qualify (partly agree), or add a new angle.
4. "How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?" → the answer reflects Text 2's view applied to Text 1's claim.

## Worked example
> **Text 1:** Some economists argue that four-day workweeks raise productivity because rested employees work more efficiently.
> **Text 2:** A two-year study by analyst Priya Raman found productivity rose under four-day weeks at software firms, but not at hospitals or factories, where output depends on hours staffed.

**How would Raman most likely respond to the economists in Text 1?**
- A) By agreeing that four-day weeks raise productivity in every industry. *(Too extreme.)*
- B) By arguing that the benefit may hold in some industries but not in others. ✅ *(Qualifies Text 1.)*
- C) By claiming four-day weeks always lower productivity. *(Contradicts her own software finding.)*
- D) By suggesting employees prefer five-day weeks. *(Off-topic.)*

lessons.title: Transitions
objectives: Name the relationship between two ideas before looking at the choices.
Pick the transition from the right relationship group.

blocks.content:
## Cover, Connect, Choose
1. **Cover** the choices.
2. **Connect:** read the sentence before the blank and the one with the blank, and name the relationship.
3. **Choose** from that group.

| Relationship | Transitions |
|---|---|
| Contrast | however, nevertheless, by contrast, still, instead |
| Cause / result | therefore, thus, consequently, as a result, hence |
| Addition | moreover, furthermore, in addition, similarly, likewise |
| Example | for example, for instance, specifically |
| Sequence | then, subsequently, finally, previously |

**Two choices that mean the same thing** (therefore / thus) signal that neither is right.

## Worked example
> Early models predicted the new bridge would ease traffic downtown. ______ congestion on nearby streets rose by 12% in the first year after it opened.

**Relationship:** prediction vs. what actually happened → **contrast**.
- A) Therefore, *(cause)*
- B) For example, *(example)*
- C) However, ✅
- D) Similarly, *(addition)*

lessons.title: Rhetorical Synthesis (Notes Questions)
objectives: Turn the question's goal into a checklist.
Pick the choice that meets every item on the checklist.

blocks.content:
## Read the goal first
These questions give you bullet-point notes and a goal: "The student wants to emphasize a difference…" **You often don't need to read the notes closely at all.** Every choice is true to the notes; only one meets the goal.

1. Read the goal.
2. Turn it into a checklist. *Emphasize a difference in size between two species* → names both species ✔ contrast word ✔ mentions size ✔
3. Check each choice against the list.

## Worked example
**Notes:**
- The Varga beetle and the Lumen beetle both live in the Teral Forest.
- The Varga beetle is about 2 cm long.
- The Lumen beetle is about 6 cm long.
- Both feed on decaying wood.

**Goal:** emphasize a difference in size between the two beetles.
- A) Both the Varga and Lumen beetles feed on decaying wood in the Teral Forest. *(A similarity.)*
- B) The Lumen beetle is about 6 cm long. *(Only one beetle.)*
- C) While the Varga beetle is about 2 cm long, the Lumen beetle is roughly three times that length. ✅
- D) The Varga beetle lives in the Teral Forest. *(Wrong attribute, one beetle.)*

units.title: Standard English Conventions
units.summary: Sentence boundaries, punctuation, agreement, tense and modifiers.

lessons.title: Sentence Boundaries: Joining Complete Sentences
objectives: Use the Split Test to see whether two parts are complete sentences.
Join complete sentences correctly and spot comma splices.

blocks.content:
## The Split Test
Put your finger at the blank. Can the part before it stand alone as a sentence? Can the part after it? If **both** can, they're two complete sentences, and only these can join them:
- a **period** (.)
- a **semicolon** (;)
- **comma + FANBOYS** (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
- a **colon** (:) when the second part explains the first

A **comma alone** is a comma splice. **Fake joiners** like however, therefore, then, and moreover can't join sentences with just a comma: "…; however, …" is right, "…, however, …" is a splice.

**Semicolon = period** for joining sentences. If both appear as choices, and nothing else is different, neither is right.

## Worked example
> The orchestra rehearsed for months ______ the premiere was canceled because of a storm.
Split Test: both sides are complete.
- A) months, *(comma splice)*
- B) months, but ✅
- C) months, however *(fake joiner after a comma)*
- D) months *(run-on)*

blocks.title: Our rule
blocks.content: Trust the Split Test, not your ear.

lessons.title: Punctuation Inside Sentences: Extra Information, Colons and Dashes
objectives: Set off extra (non-essential) information with matching marks.
Use colons correctly before lists and explanations.
Know when NO punctuation is correct.

blocks.content:
## Extra information
- **Removal test:** if you can delete the phrase and the sentence still works and means the same, it's extra information.
- **Close with the same mark that opened it:** comma…comma, dash…dash, parentheses.
- Essential information (it identifies *which* one) takes **no** commas: "The student **who won the award** spoke first."

## Colons
A colon needs a **complete sentence before it**. After it comes a list, an explanation, or an example.

## When no punctuation is right
- Never between a **subject and its verb**.
- Never between a **verb and its object**.
- Never before a list that follows "such as," "including," or a verb directly.

## Worked example
> The painter Rosa Linde ______ known for her bright murals ______ moved her studio to the coast in 1998.
"known for her bright murals" is removable → **commas on both sides**: "Rosa Linde, known for her bright murals, moved…"

blocks.title: Traps to watch for
blocks.content:
- Opening with a dash and closing with a comma.
- Putting a colon after an incomplete clause ("The kit includes: …").
- A comma between a long subject and its verb.

lessons.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
objectives: Find the true subject by crossing out the middle.
Match singular subjects with singular verbs, plural with plural.

blocks.content:
## Cross out the middle
Cross out prepositional phrases ("of the…", "in the…") and anything between commas. Match the verb to what's left.
> The **collection** of rare maps from several archives **is** on display.

## Tricky subjects
| Singular | Plural |
|---|---|
| each, every, either, neither | A and B |
| the number of… | a number of… |
| one team, one committee, one company | several, both, many |

"Along with," "as well as" and "together with" don't make a subject plural.

## Worked example
> The results of the survey, along with several interviews, ______ that residents want more parks.
Cross out "of the survey" and "along with several interviews": **The results suggest**.

blocks.title: Our rule
blocks.content: Cross out the middle, then match the verb to what's left.

lessons.title: Pronouns and Possessives
objectives: Match pronouns to their antecedents in number.
Use apostrophes correctly for possession and contractions.

blocks.content:
## Pronoun agreement
- **One** thing (including one company, team or committee) → **it / its**.
- **More than one** → **they / their**.
- Find the noun the pronoun replaces; it may be a sentence back.

## Apostrophes
| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| its | belongs to it |
| it's | it is / it has |
| their / there / they're | belongs to them / a place / they are |
| scientist's | one scientist owns it |
| scientists' | several scientists own it |
| scientists | plural, no ownership: no apostrophe |

## Worked example
> The research team published ______ findings after reviewing ______ data for two years.
"Team" is one group → **its findings … its data**.

lessons.title: Verb Tense and Verb Form
objectives: Choose tense from timeline clues and surrounding verbs.
Make sure every sentence has a main (finite) verb.

blocks.content:
## Tense
- **Clue words set the tense:** "in 1905" → past; "since 2010" → present perfect (has/have + verb); "by the time she arrived" → past perfect (had + verb).
- **No clue?** Match the other verbs in the passage.

## Form
- Every sentence needs a **main verb**. "-ing" words and "to + verb" alone can't be the main verb.
> ✘ The new library, which opened last spring, **offering** free classes.
> ✔ The new library, which opened last spring, **offers** free classes.

## Worked example
> In 1921, the engineer ______ a design for a lighter bicycle frame.
"In 1921" → simple past: **submitted**. Not "has submitted" (present perfect doesn't go with a finished past date).

lessons.title: Modifiers
objectives: Make sure an opening phrase describes the noun right after the comma.

blocks.content:
## The rule
An opening descriptive phrase must be followed **immediately** by the person or thing it describes.
> ✘ Walking through the museum, **the paintings** impressed Maya. *(The paintings weren't walking.)*
> ✔ Walking through the museum, **Maya** was impressed by the paintings.

## How the SAT tests it
The blank comes right after the comma. Ask: **who or what** is doing the opening phrase? That noun goes first.
Traps: a possessive ("Maya's visit…"), passive voice that puts the wrong noun first, or the right noun buried later in the sentence.

## Worked example
> Having studied the glacier for a decade, ______
- A) the glacier's retreat was documented by geologist Arno Pike. *(The retreat didn't study anything.)*
- B) geologist Arno Pike documented the glacier's retreat. ✅
- C) Arno Pike's study documented the retreat. *(A possessive: the study didn't study.)*
- D) the retreat of the glacier surprised geologist Arno Pike. *(Wrong noun first.)*

lessons.title: Pacing and Question Order
objectives: Pace a 32-minute module.
Decide when to skip and come back.

blocks.content:
## Pacing
- About **71 seconds per question**. Grammar questions (Unit 4) often take 30–40 seconds; save the extra time for evidence and inference questions.
- **Two passes:** answer, or mark for review and move on after about 90 seconds.
- **No penalty for guessing.** Never leave a blank.
- Module 1 decides your Module 2. Accuracy there is worth the time.

## A plan that works for many students
1. Go in order but skip any question still unclear after ~90 seconds.
2. Make sure you reach the grammar and transitions questions: they're the fastest points.
3. Use the remaining time on flagged questions.

lessons.title: Review Routine and Final Grammar Check
objectives: Use practice tests and an error log to target weak question types.
Review every grammar rule in one sitting before test day.

blocks.content:
## Practice-test routine
1. Take a full Bluebook practice test every 2–3 units.
2. Record answers in Coursebook's tracker.
3. For each miss, log the **question type** (Units 1–4) and the **reason**: misread the question, fell for a wrong-answer family, didn't know the rule, or ran out of time.
4. Redo misses 3 days later.

## One-page grammar checklist
- Split Test for joining sentences; semicolon = period.
- Extra information: matching marks; removal test.
- Colon needs a complete sentence before it.
- No punctuation between subject and verb.
- Cross out the middle for agreement.
- One group = it/its.
- Tense from clue words; every sentence needs a main verb.
- The noun after an opening phrase's comma is the one it describes.
